notes.text: And Isaac was forty years old — Not much is related concerning Isaac, but what had reference to his father, while he lived, and to his sons afterward; for Isaac seems not to have been a man of action, nor much tried, but to have spent his day, in quietness and silence.

And Isaac intreated the Lord for his wife — Though God had promised to multiply his family, he prayed for it; for God's promises must not supersede but encourage our prayers, and be improved as the ground of our faith. Though he had prayed for this mercy many years, and it was not granted, yet he did not leave off praying for it.

The children struggled within her — The commotion was altogether extra-ordinary, and made her very uneasy: If it be so, or, since it is so, why am I thus? - Before the want of children was her trouble, now the struggle of the children is no less so. And she went to inquire of the Lord - Some think Melchizedek was now consulted as an oracle, or perhaps some Urim or Teraphim were now used to inquire of God by, as afterwards in the breast-plate of judgment. The word and prayer, by which we now inquire of the Lord, give great relief to those that are upon any account perplexed: it is a mighty ease to spread our case before the Lord, and ask council at his mouth.

Two nations are in thy womb — She was now big not only with two children, but two nations, which should not only in their manners greatly differ from each other, but in their interest contend with each other, and the issue of the contest should be that the elder should serve the younger, which was fulfilled in the subjection of the Edomites for many ages to the house of David.

Esau when he was born was red and hairy, as if he had been already a grown man, whence he had his name Esau, made, reared already. This was an indication of a very strong constitution, and gave cause to expect that he would be a very robust, daring, active man. But Jacob was smooth and tender as other children.

His hand took hold on Esau's heel — This signified,

1. Jacob's pursuit of the birth-right and blessing; from the first he reached forth to have catched hold of it, and if possible to have prevented his brother.

2. His prevailing for it at last: that in process of time he should gain his point. This passage is referred to Hosea xii, 3, and from hence he had his name Jacob, a supplanter.

Esau was an hunter — And a man that knew how to live by his wits, for he was a cunning hunter. A man of the field - All for the game, and never so well but as when he was in pursuit of it. And Jacob was a plain man - An honest man, that dealt fairly. And dwelt in tents - Either,

1. As a shepherd, loving that safe and silent employment of keeping sheep, to which also he bred up his children, chap. xlvi, 34. Or,

2. As a student, he frequented the tents of Melchizedek or Heber, as some understand it, to be taught by them divine things.

And Isaac loved Esau — Isaac though he was not a stirring man himself, yet he loved to have his son active. Esau knew how to please him, and shewed a great respect for him, by treating him often with venison, which won upon him more than one would have thought. But Rebekah loved him whom God loved.
Sod — That is, boiled.
Edom — That is, red.

Sell me this day thy birth-right — He cannot be excused in taking advantage of Esau's necessity, yet neither can Esau be excused who is profane, Heb. xii, 16, because for one morsel of meat he sold his birth-right. The birth-right was typical of spiritual privileges, those of the church of the first-born: Esau was now tried how he would value those, and he shews himself sensible only of present grievances: may he but get relief against them, he cares not for his birth-right. If we look on Esau's birth-right as only a temporal advantage, what he said had something of truth in it, that our worldly enjoyments, even those we are most fond of, will stand us in no stead in a dying hour. They will not put by the stroke of death, nor ease the pangs, nor remove the sting. But being of a spiritual nature, his undervaluing it, was the greatest profaneness imaginable. It is egregious folly to part with our interest in God, and Christ, and heaven, for the riches, honours, and pleasures of this world.

He did eat and drink, and rise up and went his way — Without any serious reflections upon the ill bargain he had made, or any shew of regret. Thus Esau despised his birth-right - He used no means to get the bargain revoked, made no appeal to his father about it but the bargain which his necessity had made, (supposing it were so) his profaneness confirmed, and by his subsequent neglect and contempt, he put the bargain past recall. In this chapter we have, I. Isaac in adversity, by reason of a famine in the land; which, (1.) Obliges him to change his quarters, ver 1. but, (2.) God visits him with direction and comfort, ver. 2-5. (3.) He denies his wife, and is reproved for it by Abimelech, ver. 6-11. II. Isaac in prosperity, by the blessing of God upon him, ver. 12- 14. (1.) The Philistines were envious at him, ver. 14-17. (2.) He continued industrious in his business, ver. 18-23. (3.) God appeared to him, and encouraged him, and he returned to his duty, ver. 24-25. (4.) The Philistines at length made court to him, and made a covenant with him, ver. 26-33 III. The disagreeable marriage of his son Esau was an allay to his prosperity, ver. 34. 35.

glossa.text: « And he dwelt from Hevila as far as Sur, which looketh towards Egypt, » etc. The region which Phison went about was so called from Hevila, the grandson of Noe, and it is a wilderness over against the face of Egypt. Sur also is a wilderness between Cades and Barad, stretching the desert as far as the Red Sea and the borders of Egypt.

« From Mesopotamia the sister of Laban. » A barren region, which is so called in Greek because it lies in the middle between two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. For μέσος is said *middle,* ποταμὸς *a river*; hence hippopotamus, that is, a river horse.

« And he besought . . . but the little ones struggled in her womb, » etc. ((HIER.)) For the stirring or the collision the LXX put « they played » or « they kicked back: » Aquila, « the sons fought in her womb. » Symmachus, « they were borne upon the surface after the likeness of a ship. » ((GREG., Dial. I, 8.)) The things which the saints effect by praying, etc., *as far as* for he in whom God had predestined to multiply the seed of Abraham obtained by prayer that he might have sons.

« Who heard her. » ((CHRYSOST.)) Think not that he obtained forthwith and at once what he desired: for he continued twenty years praying and beseeching God. For as he taught us how many years he had when he took Rebecca (namely forty), so he assigned to us of how many years Isaac was when sons were born to him. « He was sixty years old, he says, when the little ones were born. »

« And she went, » etc., ((AUG., Quaest. in Gen., tom. III.)) It is asked: whither did she go, since there were as yet no prophets or priests of the tabernacle or of the temple of the Lord? Perhaps to the place where Abraham set up an altar. But how answers were given there, Scripture is silent; was it through some priest? And it is a wonder, if there was one, that he was not named, and that no mention of priests was made. Perhaps there, when they had laid their desires before God in prayer, they slept, that they might be admonished through a dream: or Melchisedech was yet living, whose excellence was so great that it was doubted whether he were a man or an angel. Or perhaps even at that time there were men of God, in whom God could be consulted. Whichever of these, or perhaps somewhat else, it was. Rebecca however according to the Scripture consulted the Lord, and deserved his answer.

« Who answering said: Two nations, » etc. ((AUG.)) By historical propriety the answer is found fulfilled, when for Israel's sake, that is, Jacob's, the younger son overcame the Idumeans, that is, the nation which Esau propagated, and made them tributaries through David; which they were for a long time, until king Joram ((IV Reg. VIII)). For then the Idumeans rebelled, and shook the yoke from their neck, as Isaac had prophesied when he blessed the younger before the elder, and said this same thing to the elder, when he afterwards blessed him.

« The time was now come, » etc. ((HIER.)) Where we have put « hairy », in the Hebrew there stands *seyr* ( ); whence Esau, as we read elsewhere, was called *seyr,* that is, hairy.

« Forthwith the other, » etc. ((ISID.)) That this was done figuratively is known even to the Jews who believe not: how the people of the Church overcame the people of the Synagogue, and the people of the Jews, the greater in time, served the lesser people of the Christians.

((BED. in hoc cap., tom. II.)) In individual men also this may be said. « Two nations and two peoples » are within us, namely of the vices and of the virtues; the one lesser, the other greater: for the evil are more than the good, and the vices more than the virtues. Yet the people overcomes the people, « and the elder shall serve the younger, » namely the flesh the spirit, and the vices the virtues. Esau goes before, red, and all hairy as a skin: then comes forth Jacob holding his brother's heel; for the former people, polluted with the blood of the prophets and of Christ, was encompassed with the squalor of sin and of wickedness: whose heel the younger held, because the lesser people overcame the greater.

« Esau became, » etc. ((GREG.)) It signifies the life of those who, poured out upon outward pleasures, follow the flesh. He is also called a husbandman, because lovers of the world cultivate outward things the more, the more they leave their own inward things untilled.

« Simple. » ((GREG.)) Because simple men shun to be scattered abroad by outward cares, and abide in thought and in the dwelling of conscience. For he dwells in tents who binds himself within the secret places of the mind, lest, while he gapes outwards after many things, he depart from himself, estranged in thought.

« And Jacob boiled, » etc. ((HIERON.)) *Red* or *tawny:* in Hebrew it is called *Edom*: and from this, that Esau sold his birthright for red food, he received the name of the tawny, that is, of *Edom*.

« To whom Jacob said, » etc. ((ISID.)) That Esau sold his birthright to his younger brother for food, and was afterwards deprived of the paternal blessing promised him, signifies the Jewish people: who in Exodus is called the firstborn son of God, and for the gains of the world not only lost the honour of his primacy, but also deserved not to obtain the prepared reward of the heavenly kingdom. Whence by way of reproach it is said Matth. XII: « The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and shall be given to the Gentiles, » etc. But the birthright was a priestly garment, clothed in which the elder-born offered victims to God with their father's blessing, as pontiffs: of which gift, through desire of earthly love, the Jews were bereft, together with the glory of the kingdom to come.

« Esau swore, » etc. ((GREG., lib. XXX, Moral., c. 13.)) But it is to be known that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways, etc., *as far as* and not the things which the lust of eating suggests.

notes.text: Offerings — The sacrifices of prayer and praise.
Is — Exposed to perpetual danger.

There is therefore now no condemnation — Either for things present or past. Now he comes to deliverance and liberty. The apostle here resumes the thread of his discourse, which was interrupted, chap. vii, 7.
The law of the Spirit — That is, the gospel. Hath freed me from the law of sin and death - That is, the Mosaic dispensation.

For what the law — Of Moses. Could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh - Incapable of conquering our evil nature. If it could, God needed not to have sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh - We with our sinful flesh were devoted to death. But God sending his own Son, in the likeness of that flesh, though pure from sin, condemned that sin which was in our flesh; gave sentence, that sin should be destroyed, and the believer wholly delivered from it.

That the righteousness of the law — The holiness it required, described, ver. 11. Might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit - Who are guided in all our thoughts, words, and actions, not by corrupt nature, but by the Spirit of God. From this place St. Paul describes primarily the state of believers, and that of unbelievers only to illustrate this.

They that are after the flesh — Who remain under the guidance of corrupt nature. Mind the things of the flesh - Have their thoughts and affections fixed on such things as gratify corrupt nature; namely, on things visible and temporal; on things of the earth, on pleasure, (of sense or imagination,) praise, or riches. But they who are after the Spirit - Who are under his guidance. Mind the things of the Spirit - Think of, relish, love things invisible, eternal; the things which the Spirit hath revealed, which he works in us, moves us to, and promises to give us.

For to be carnally minded — That is, to mind the things of the flesh. Is death - The sure mark of spiritual death, and the way to death everlasting. But to be spiritually minded - That is, to mind the things of the Spirit. Is life - A sure mark of spiritual life, and the way to life everlasting. And attended with peace - The peace of God, which is the foretaste of life everlasting; and peace with God, opposite to the enmity mentioned in the next verse.
Enmity against God — His existence, power, and providence.
They who are in the flesh — Under the government of it.

In the Spirit — Under his government. If any man have not the Spirit of Christ - Dwelling and governing in him. He is none of his - He is not a member of Christ; not a Christian; not in a state of salvation. A plain, express declaration, which admits of no exception. He that hath ears to hear, let him hear!

Now if Christ be in you — Where the Spirit of Christ is, there is Christ. The body indeed is dead - Devoted to death. Because of sin - Heretofore committed. But the Spirit is life - Already truly alive. Because of righteousness - Now attained. From ver. 13, St. Paul, having finished what he had begun, chap. vi, 1, describes purely the state of believers.

glossa.text:
*Nothing therefore now.* Even if before, not now: since [they are] in Christ. *Nothing of damnation.* Because through the grace of baptism and the laver of regeneration there has been loosed both the guilt itself with which thou wast born, and whatsoever thou hast committed before.

((AUG.)) Even if they have desires of the flesh to which they do not consent, etc., *as far as* but this good regeneration has wrought.

*For the law of the spirit.* Here he shows by what grace delivers, namely by the Holy Spirit, because [it is] *the law of the spirit.* It is the Holy Spirit who teaches what is to be done and what is not, who is the giver of life, and this through Christ who gives the Spirit: and he sets forth how, in Christ.

*For what was impossible.* He shows how in Christ the deliverance was made. *Through the flesh.* Through carnality, which was rebelling, and on the hearing of the law was the more incited; thus the law of the letter was made weak through the flesh, and therefore it was impossible for it to deliver from the law of sin and of death.

*Sending his own Son. ((AUG.))* Not where he was not: who is everywhere, etc., *as far as* because he appeared visible to the world.

*Into the likeness,* etc. Not into sinful flesh; because his mother conceived him not by concupiscence but by grace. It was not therefore sinful, because it was neither conceived in the concupiscence of lust, nor had in itself the cause of sin, nor did he sin in it. In punishment therefore it is like to ours, not in the quality of sin.

 *And of sin. ((ORIG.))* That is: By the victim of his own flesh which he offered on the altar of the cross, he condemned sin, and reduced it to nothing in his own flesh.

*He condemned.* That is, he destroyed the devil, that is, for the sin which he works in the flesh of Christ. Or sin, that is, he condemned the tinder proceeding from the sin of Adam, that is, he weakened it.
*That the justification.* So is sin condemned through Christ that the justice which the law of Moses promised might be consummated.

*For they that are according to the flesh.* He that walketh according to the flesh is not just, because neither is he who is according to it. Why not? because he desires carnal things as the highest goods, which is repugnant to justice.

*For the prudence.* He who savours these things which are of the flesh is not just; for the prudence of the flesh is death. *Life and peace.* Life indeed referred to this, *the affection of the flesh is death;* but peace to that which follows: *the affection of the flesh is enmity toward God.*

*Because the wisdom of the flesh.* By enumerating these things he deters from obedience to the flesh.

*It is an enemy.* While it thinks God can do nothing beyond what is seen in the natures of things.

*If yet.* He speaks ambiguously, because they are not yet of perfect faith, but there is hope of their being perfected. *The Spirit of God.* The Spirit of Christ, because the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are the same.

*The body indeed.* By the name of the body he signifies the whole man, as Ezekiel conversely by the name of the soul, when he says: *The soul that hath sinned,* etc. And the sense is: If the spirit of Christ is in you, although the body be dead, that is, although the man be dead because of sins, that is, in sins, yet the spirit, that is, the soul which had been ungodly, lives: because it is joined to God, who is life, and this because of justification, that is, the remission of sins, which is from the Holy Spirit. *Dead,* he says, not mortal. For before sin the body was animal, that is, mortal, namely able to die. But which it was not necessary to die: now it is called dead because of sin, that is, because it is necessary to die. *Because of sin* to be shunned, this weakness is kept back, that thereby he may the more fear to sin.

*But if the Spirit. ((AUG.))* Mark that the Holy Spirit, etc., *as far as* even as who shall declare the generation of the Son?

*He shall quicken also your mortal. ((ID.))* Behold the fourth act. In the first action, etc., *as far as* because we had forsaken God who is above us.

*Mortal.* Not dead, because in the resurrection, when this mortal shall put on immortality, not only the necessity of dying, which it now has because of sin, but not even the mortality which the animal body had before sin, shall remain.

*Because of him that dwelleth.* It appears most evidently that man deserved, because of sin, the death not only of the spirit but also of the body, and that through the Holy Spirit both were delivered by Christ.

notes.text: Mark iv, 1; Luke viii, 4.
He went into the vessel — Which constantly waited upon him, while he was on the sea coast.

In parables — The word is here taken in its proper sense, for apt similes or comparisons. This way of speaking, extremely common in the eastern countries, drew and fixed the attention of many, and occasioned the truths delivered to sink the deeper into humble and serious hearers. At the same time, by an awful mixture of justice and mercy, it hid them from the proud and careless. In this chapter our Lord delivers seven parables; directing the four former (as being of general concern) to all the people; the three latter to his disciples. Behold the sower - How exquisitely proper is this parable to be an introduction to all the rest! In this our Lord answers a very obvious and a very important question. The same sower, Christ, and the same preachers sent by him, always sow the same seed: why has it not always the same effect? He that hath ears to hear, let him hear!

And while he sowed, some seeds fell by the highway side, and the birds came and devoured them — It is observable, that our Lord points out the grand hindrances of our bearing fruit, in the same order as they occur. The first danger is, that the birds will devour the seed. If it escape this, there is then another danger, namely, lest it be scorched, and wither away. It is long after this that the thorns spring up and choke the good seed. A vast majority of those who hear the word of God, receive the seed as by the highway side. Of those who do not lose it by the birds, yet many receive it as on stony places. Many of them who receive it in a better soil, yet suffer the thorns to grow up, and choke it: so that few even of these endure to the end, and bear fruit unto perfection: yet in all these cases, it is not the will of God that hinders, but their own voluntary perverseness.
Good ground — Soft, not like that by the highway side; deep, not like the stony ground; purged, not full of thorns.

glossa.text: *On that day.* By this he indicates that this was done next in order, unless perhaps the day be put for the time, after the manner of Scripture. Mark keeps the same order. Luke passes to another matter, yet neither does he contradict this. ((RAB.)) Not only the deeds and the sayings of the Lord, but his journeys also, etc., *as far as* to which the Jews did not enter in, fixed outside in the letter.

*The crowd stood.* These are they who have lately come to hear, who are also set apart from the waves of the sea, and do not yet ascend with Christ, steeped in the heavenly mysteries which they desire.

*He spoke many things.* Because the crowd is not of one mind but of diverse wills, he speaks to them in many parables, that according to their various pleasures they may receive diverse instructions. *He that soweth.* Christ himself, who sowed among men, by himself or by his own, the word of truth which he had seen with the Father. He who was speaking sacraments to the disciples went out to sow the word of God among the crowds.

*By the way side.* The way is a mind trodden and dried up by the busy passage of evil thoughts. There the seed perishes in two ways, because it is both trampled by the passing of thoughts, as Luke says, and snatched away by the birds. The demons are called birds, either because they are of a heavenly and spiritual nature, or because they fly through the air. *And they came.* According to Luke it was trodden down by men, because it was taken away by the crooked persuasion of the wicked. *And they ate it up.* Because they stole it away from the minds of men.

*Upon stony ground.* Stony places seek to sprout quickly, but the root is not fixed, because the earth is not deep, that is, because there is little of saving desire within. In this exposition of the Lord we learn that things are not always set down in the same signification. For the rock here stands for hardness, the earth for softness of mind, the sun for the heat of persecution. Whereas elsewhere the sun is in a good sense: *The just shall shine as the sun ((Matth. XIII))*, and the rock in a foundation, for the strength of faith, and the earth for earthly thoughts. *The depth of earth.* The depth of earth is the uprightness of a mind schooled in heavenly disciplines and proved in temptations.
*Sixtyfold.* Because in the number six the adornment of the world was completed, by this good working is signified.
*He that hath ears to hear.* As often as this admonition is interposed in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse of John, it is intimated that what is said is mystical.

echoes.text: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn, and I have said to you, “Let my son go, that he may serve me”; and you have refused to let him go. Behold, I will kill your son, your firstborn.’”
echoes.note: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn' grounds the sonship/adoption language of vv.14-17; the Spirit constitutes believers as 'children of God,' transferring Israel's sonship status to those led by the Spirit.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The Spirit enabling 'the ordinance of the law' to be 'fulfilled in us' (v.4) draws on the new-covenant promise to write the Torah on the heart, internalizing the law by divine agency rather than external command.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit within you and cause you to walk in my statutes' undergirds vv.4-9: the indwelling Spirit (vv.9,11) produces obedience and 'walking according to the Spirit'; the verbal cluster Spirit-indwelling-walking-statutes is distinctive to Ezekiel.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit in you and you shall live' (the dry-bones vision) lies behind v.11, where the Spirit who raised Jesus 'will also give life to your mortal bodies'; Spirit-giving-life-to-dead-bodies is the precise Ezekielian figure.

echoes.text: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]
echoes.note: 'The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace' and 'if you live after the flesh you must die... by the Spirit... you will live' (vv.6,13) reframe the covenantal life-and-death choice of Moses' exhortation set before Israel.

echoes.text: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'When Israel was a child I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son' supplies the adopted-son-led-by-God motif (vv.14-15); the tender father-son relation undergirds the cry 'Abba! Father!'

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: 'In the place where it was said to them, You are not my people, it shall be said, You are children of the living God' anticipates 'these are children of God' / 'we are children of God' (vv.14,16); Paul cites this very text in Romans 9:26.

echoes.text: if the anointed priest sins so as to bring guilt on the people, then let him offer for his sin, which he has sinned, a young bull without defect to Yahweh for a sin offering.
echoes.note: 'for sin' (peri hamartias) in v.3 reproduces the Septuagint's standing phrase for the sin offering; God's sending his Son 'for sin' figurally casts Christ in the role of the Levitical purification sacrifice that 'condemns sin in the flesh.'

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.”
echoes.note: The flesh/Spirit antithesis (vv.5-9), where 'flesh' marks mortal humanity opposed to God's enduring Spirit, faintly recalls 'My Spirit will not abide in man forever, for he is flesh.'

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: 'The spirit is alive' / God giving 'life to your mortal bodies' (vv.10-11) faintly evokes the breath of life animating dust-formed Adam, now reapplied as resurrection-life by the Spirit.

echoes.text: For you are our Father, though Abraham doesn’t know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us: you, Yahweh, are our Father; our Redeemer from everlasting is your name.
echoes.note: 'You, O LORD, are our Father' — Israel's corporate address of God as Father — stands behind the Spirit-prompted filial cry 'Abba! Father!' (v.15).

echoes.text: “But I said, ‘How I would put you among the children, and give you a pleasant land, a goodly heritage of the armies of the nations!’ and I said, ‘You shall call me “My Father”, and shall not turn away from following me.’
echoes.note: 'I thought you would call me My Father and would not turn from following me' — God's hope that adopted Israel address him as Father — resonates with the adoptive cry of v.15.

echoes.text: I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.
echoes.note: The covenant formula 'I will... be your God, and you shall be my people,' realized through the indwelling Spirit (vv.9-16), faintly underlies the divine-belonging and sonship affirmed by the Spirit's testimony.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: The word/seed that goes out from God's mouth and does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, yielding seed and bread; the sower-and-word matrix governs the parable, made explicit in the later interpretation (v.19, 'the word of the Kingdom').

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.
echoes.note: 'Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns' — the contrast of receptive ground vs. thorn-choked soil maps directly onto Jesus' soils; thorns that choke recur in v.7, 22.

echoes.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.
echoes.note: 'Sow righteousness... break up your fallow ground' — agricultural sowing-and-reaping imagery for response to God's word; thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him.
echoes.note: Isaac sows and reaps a hundredfold (LXX 'hekatosteuousan') in the same year — the only clear OT 'hundredfold' agricultural blessing, possible backdrop for the good soil's hundredfold yield (v.8).

echoes.text: For as the husbandman sows much seed upon the ground, and plants many trees, and yet not all that is sown shall come up in due season, neither shall all that is planted take root: even so those who are sown in the world shall not all be saved.
echoes.note: Second Temple (4 Ezra): the farmer sows much seed but not all that is sown takes root or is saved — a near-contemporary Jewish sower parable of differential reception; cf. also 2 Esdras 9:31.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The Song of the Vineyard: God plants/sows expecting fruit and is disappointed by a barren yield; thematic kinship with fruit-bearing soils but no verbal overlap.

notes.text: The snow — Which in its season contributes to the fruitfulness of the earth. Returneth not - Without effect. And bread - That it may bring forth store of bread-corn, both for mens present supplies, and for seed for the next year.
My word — My promises, concerning the pardon of the greatest sinners. Void - Without success.
Therefore — Ye shall be released from your bondage. Peace - Safely and triumphantly. Clap - There shall be a general rejoicing, so that even the senseless creatures shall seem to rejoice with you.

Instead — Whereas your land was filled with thorns and briars, as was foretold, they shall be rooted out, and it shall be planted with fir-trees and myrtle-trees, and such other trees, as are useful either for fruit or for delight. The church shall be delivered from pernicious things, and replenished with all divine graces and blessings. It - This wonderful change shall bring much honour to God. A sign - For a monument, of God's infinite power, and faithfulness, and love to his people to all succeeding generations. The blessedness of the Godly without any respect of persons, ver. 1-8. Blind watchmen shall be destroyed, ver. 9-12.

glossa.text:
*And how.* ((ID.)) By another likeness he shows that he is abundant in pardoning.

*Bread to the eater.* Whence Solomon: *Cast thy bread upon the waters, for in the multitude of days thou shalt find it ,* that is, pour out the bread of thy doctrine and spiritual grace upon all, because in the last day thou shalt receive rewards
*It shall not return.* But after it has fulfilled my will upon earth, it shall return and sit at my right hand, according to that, *Sit thou at my right hand,* etc.
*The mountains,* namely the souls of the saints, which for the variety of their virtues are called mountains and hills.

*Instead of the nard.* Nard, full of prickles and of stings. The fir, tall, lofty, apt for building houses, rich in pitch.

*And the Lord shall be.* Others. And the Lord shall be for a name and for an everlasting sign which shall not fail.

notes.text: River — With rain, which he very significantly calls a river for its plenty, and the river of God, of God's immediate providing. Them - The inhabitants of the earth. Provided - Or, disposed, the earth, which without this would be hard and barren.
Bringest down — For the rain dissolves the high and hard clods of earth.
Wilderness — Which though neglected by men, are furnished with food for beasts.

Sing — They are abundantly satisfied with thy goodness, and in their manner sing forth the praise of their benefactor. The psalmist calls on all people to praise God, for his sovereign power over the whole creation, ver. 1-7. For his special favour to his people, ver. 8-12. Praises him for his goodness to himself in particular, ver. 13-20. To the chief musician, A song or psalm.

glossa.text:
*Thou hast visited the earth and hast inebriated it.* Through preachers wilt thou do this, for within thou teachest those to whom they preach.

*A river.* Of the deep, for the receiving, it is filled with waters, with the gifts of the Holy Ghost, for thou hast prepared food. *The river of God.* ((CAS.)) The mercy of God is compared to a river in full flood, etc., *as far as* as it is disposed by him, without whom nothing is done there.

*Its streams.* The Apostles and others, who drank of the river. *Inebriate them,* that they may suffice for themselves and for others. *Multiply,* that through successions preaching may not fail. *The crown of the year,* the whole world, where the Church is. *Its streams. ((Ibid.)) Thou hast prepared,* etc. And, O Lord, etc., *as far as* whereby the Word of God grows. *The crown of the year. ((Ibid.))* Because the glory of victory belongs to him who conquers the devil. *Of thy bounty,* etc. ((AUG.)) Let no one glory in his own merits.

*Thy fields shall be filled.* ((CASS., AUG.)) Men, because of their evenness, that is, the just. *The hills,* because God raises up the humble *The desert:* all the Gentiles, to whom no prophet was sent.
*The beautiful places of the wilderness shall grow fat.* When the Apostles came to them, through whom they were made comely.

*Valleys. ((Ibid.))* Lowly peoples shall bring forth much fruit. *They shall cry out. ((Ibid.))* *Clamabuut* Not in blasphemy, but in a hymn, thence they abound with corn.

This psalm is sung at the funerals of the faithful, because it treats of the return from the Babylon of this world to the heavenly country, to which the saints, led forth from the flesh at their death, happily pass over, receiving the single robe, until in the resurrection they be glorified with the robe of a twofold beatitude.

notes.text: There is therefore now no condemnation — Either for things present or past. Now he comes to deliverance and liberty. The apostle here resumes the thread of his discourse, which was interrupted, chap. vii, 7.
The law of the Spirit — That is, the gospel. Hath freed me from the law of sin and death - That is, the Mosaic dispensation.

For what the law — Of Moses. Could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh - Incapable of conquering our evil nature. If it could, God needed not to have sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh - We with our sinful flesh were devoted to death. But God sending his own Son, in the likeness of that flesh, though pure from sin, condemned that sin which was in our flesh; gave sentence, that sin should be destroyed, and the believer wholly delivered from it.

That the righteousness of the law — The holiness it required, described, ver. 11. Might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit - Who are guided in all our thoughts, words, and actions, not by corrupt nature, but by the Spirit of God. From this place St. Paul describes primarily the state of believers, and that of unbelievers only to illustrate this.

They that are after the flesh — Who remain under the guidance of corrupt nature. Mind the things of the flesh - Have their thoughts and affections fixed on such things as gratify corrupt nature; namely, on things visible and temporal; on things of the earth, on pleasure, (of sense or imagination,) praise, or riches. But they who are after the Spirit - Who are under his guidance. Mind the things of the Spirit - Think of, relish, love things invisible, eternal; the things which the Spirit hath revealed, which he works in us, moves us to, and promises to give us.

For to be carnally minded — That is, to mind the things of the flesh. Is death - The sure mark of spiritual death, and the way to death everlasting. But to be spiritually minded - That is, to mind the things of the Spirit. Is life - A sure mark of spiritual life, and the way to life everlasting. And attended with peace - The peace of God, which is the foretaste of life everlasting; and peace with God, opposite to the enmity mentioned in the next verse.
Enmity against God — His existence, power, and providence.
They who are in the flesh — Under the government of it.

In the Spirit — Under his government. If any man have not the Spirit of Christ - Dwelling and governing in him. He is none of his - He is not a member of Christ; not a Christian; not in a state of salvation. A plain, express declaration, which admits of no exception. He that hath ears to hear, let him hear!

Now if Christ be in you — Where the Spirit of Christ is, there is Christ. The body indeed is dead - Devoted to death. Because of sin - Heretofore committed. But the Spirit is life - Already truly alive. Because of righteousness - Now attained. From ver. 13, St. Paul, having finished what he had begun, chap. vi, 1, describes purely the state of believers.

glossa.text:
*Nothing therefore now.* Even if before, not now: since [they are] in Christ. *Nothing of damnation.* Because through the grace of baptism and the laver of regeneration there has been loosed both the guilt itself with which thou wast born, and whatsoever thou hast committed before.

((AUG.)) Even if they have desires of the flesh to which they do not consent, etc., *as far as* but this good regeneration has wrought.

*For the law of the spirit.* Here he shows by what grace delivers, namely by the Holy Spirit, because [it is] *the law of the spirit.* It is the Holy Spirit who teaches what is to be done and what is not, who is the giver of life, and this through Christ who gives the Spirit: and he sets forth how, in Christ.

*For what was impossible.* He shows how in Christ the deliverance was made. *Through the flesh.* Through carnality, which was rebelling, and on the hearing of the law was the more incited; thus the law of the letter was made weak through the flesh, and therefore it was impossible for it to deliver from the law of sin and of death.

*Sending his own Son. ((AUG.))* Not where he was not: who is everywhere, etc., *as far as* because he appeared visible to the world.

*Into the likeness,* etc. Not into sinful flesh; because his mother conceived him not by concupiscence but by grace. It was not therefore sinful, because it was neither conceived in the concupiscence of lust, nor had in itself the cause of sin, nor did he sin in it. In punishment therefore it is like to ours, not in the quality of sin.

 *And of sin. ((ORIG.))* That is: By the victim of his own flesh which he offered on the altar of the cross, he condemned sin, and reduced it to nothing in his own flesh.

*He condemned.* That is, he destroyed the devil, that is, for the sin which he works in the flesh of Christ. Or sin, that is, he condemned the tinder proceeding from the sin of Adam, that is, he weakened it.
*That the justification.* So is sin condemned through Christ that the justice which the law of Moses promised might be consummated.

*For they that are according to the flesh.* He that walketh according to the flesh is not just, because neither is he who is according to it. Why not? because he desires carnal things as the highest goods, which is repugnant to justice.

*For the prudence.* He who savours these things which are of the flesh is not just; for the prudence of the flesh is death. *Life and peace.* Life indeed referred to this, *the affection of the flesh is death;* but peace to that which follows: *the affection of the flesh is enmity toward God.*

*Because the wisdom of the flesh.* By enumerating these things he deters from obedience to the flesh.

*It is an enemy.* While it thinks God can do nothing beyond what is seen in the natures of things.

*If yet.* He speaks ambiguously, because they are not yet of perfect faith, but there is hope of their being perfected. *The Spirit of God.* The Spirit of Christ, because the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are the same.

*The body indeed.* By the name of the body he signifies the whole man, as Ezekiel conversely by the name of the soul, when he says: *The soul that hath sinned,* etc. And the sense is: If the spirit of Christ is in you, although the body be dead, that is, although the man be dead because of sins, that is, in sins, yet the spirit, that is, the soul which had been ungodly, lives: because it is joined to God, who is life, and this because of justification, that is, the remission of sins, which is from the Holy Spirit. *Dead,* he says, not mortal. For before sin the body was animal, that is, mortal, namely able to die. But which it was not necessary to die: now it is called dead because of sin, that is, because it is necessary to die. *Because of sin* to be shunned, this weakness is kept back, that thereby he may the more fear to sin.

*But if the Spirit. ((AUG.))* Mark that the Holy Spirit, etc., *as far as* even as who shall declare the generation of the Son?

*He shall quicken also your mortal. ((ID.))* Behold the fourth act. In the first action, etc., *as far as* because we had forsaken God who is above us.

*Mortal.* Not dead, because in the resurrection, when this mortal shall put on immortality, not only the necessity of dying, which it now has because of sin, but not even the mortality which the animal body had before sin, shall remain.

*Because of him that dwelleth.* It appears most evidently that man deserved, because of sin, the death not only of the spirit but also of the body, and that through the Holy Spirit both were delivered by Christ.

notes.text: Mark iv, 1; Luke viii, 4.
He went into the vessel — Which constantly waited upon him, while he was on the sea coast.

In parables — The word is here taken in its proper sense, for apt similes or comparisons. This way of speaking, extremely common in the eastern countries, drew and fixed the attention of many, and occasioned the truths delivered to sink the deeper into humble and serious hearers. At the same time, by an awful mixture of justice and mercy, it hid them from the proud and careless. In this chapter our Lord delivers seven parables; directing the four former (as being of general concern) to all the people; the three latter to his disciples. Behold the sower - How exquisitely proper is this parable to be an introduction to all the rest! In this our Lord answers a very obvious and a very important question. The same sower, Christ, and the same preachers sent by him, always sow the same seed: why has it not always the same effect? He that hath ears to hear, let him hear!

And while he sowed, some seeds fell by the highway side, and the birds came and devoured them — It is observable, that our Lord points out the grand hindrances of our bearing fruit, in the same order as they occur. The first danger is, that the birds will devour the seed. If it escape this, there is then another danger, namely, lest it be scorched, and wither away. It is long after this that the thorns spring up and choke the good seed. A vast majority of those who hear the word of God, receive the seed as by the highway side. Of those who do not lose it by the birds, yet many receive it as on stony places. Many of them who receive it in a better soil, yet suffer the thorns to grow up, and choke it: so that few even of these endure to the end, and bear fruit unto perfection: yet in all these cases, it is not the will of God that hinders, but their own voluntary perverseness.
Good ground — Soft, not like that by the highway side; deep, not like the stony ground; purged, not full of thorns.

glossa.text: *On that day.* By this he indicates that this was done next in order, unless perhaps the day be put for the time, after the manner of Scripture. Mark keeps the same order. Luke passes to another matter, yet neither does he contradict this. ((RAB.)) Not only the deeds and the sayings of the Lord, but his journeys also, etc., *as far as* to which the Jews did not enter in, fixed outside in the letter.

*The crowd stood.* These are they who have lately come to hear, who are also set apart from the waves of the sea, and do not yet ascend with Christ, steeped in the heavenly mysteries which they desire.

*He spoke many things.* Because the crowd is not of one mind but of diverse wills, he speaks to them in many parables, that according to their various pleasures they may receive diverse instructions. *He that soweth.* Christ himself, who sowed among men, by himself or by his own, the word of truth which he had seen with the Father. He who was speaking sacraments to the disciples went out to sow the word of God among the crowds.

*By the way side.* The way is a mind trodden and dried up by the busy passage of evil thoughts. There the seed perishes in two ways, because it is both trampled by the passing of thoughts, as Luke says, and snatched away by the birds. The demons are called birds, either because they are of a heavenly and spiritual nature, or because they fly through the air. *And they came.* According to Luke it was trodden down by men, because it was taken away by the crooked persuasion of the wicked. *And they ate it up.* Because they stole it away from the minds of men.

*Upon stony ground.* Stony places seek to sprout quickly, but the root is not fixed, because the earth is not deep, that is, because there is little of saving desire within. In this exposition of the Lord we learn that things are not always set down in the same signification. For the rock here stands for hardness, the earth for softness of mind, the sun for the heat of persecution. Whereas elsewhere the sun is in a good sense: *The just shall shine as the sun ((Matth. XIII))*, and the rock in a foundation, for the strength of faith, and the earth for earthly thoughts. *The depth of earth.* The depth of earth is the uprightness of a mind schooled in heavenly disciplines and proved in temptations.
*Sixtyfold.* Because in the number six the adornment of the world was completed, by this good working is signified.
*He that hath ears to hear.* As often as this admonition is interposed in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse of John, it is intimated that what is said is mystical.

echoes.text: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn, and I have said to you, “Let my son go, that he may serve me”; and you have refused to let him go. Behold, I will kill your son, your firstborn.’”
echoes.note: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn' grounds the sonship/adoption language of vv.14-17; the Spirit constitutes believers as 'children of God,' transferring Israel's sonship status to those led by the Spirit.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The Spirit enabling 'the ordinance of the law' to be 'fulfilled in us' (v.4) draws on the new-covenant promise to write the Torah on the heart, internalizing the law by divine agency rather than external command.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit within you and cause you to walk in my statutes' undergirds vv.4-9: the indwelling Spirit (vv.9,11) produces obedience and 'walking according to the Spirit'; the verbal cluster Spirit-indwelling-walking-statutes is distinctive to Ezekiel.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit in you and you shall live' (the dry-bones vision) lies behind v.11, where the Spirit who raised Jesus 'will also give life to your mortal bodies'; Spirit-giving-life-to-dead-bodies is the precise Ezekielian figure.

echoes.text: Behold, I have set before you this day life and prosperity, and death and evil. For I command you this day to love Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his ordinances, that you may live and multiply, and that Yahweh your God may bless you in the land where you go in to possess it. But if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce to […]
echoes.note: 'The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace' and 'if you live after the flesh you must die... by the Spirit... you will live' (vv.6,13) reframe the covenantal life-and-death choice of Moses' exhortation set before Israel.

echoes.text: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
echoes.note: 'When Israel was a child I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son' supplies the adopted-son-led-by-God motif (vv.14-15); the tender father-son relation undergirds the cry 'Abba! Father!'

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: 'In the place where it was said to them, You are not my people, it shall be said, You are children of the living God' anticipates 'these are children of God' / 'we are children of God' (vv.14,16); Paul cites this very text in Romans 9:26.

echoes.text: if the anointed priest sins so as to bring guilt on the people, then let him offer for his sin, which he has sinned, a young bull without defect to Yahweh for a sin offering.
echoes.note: 'for sin' (peri hamartias) in v.3 reproduces the Septuagint's standing phrase for the sin offering; God's sending his Son 'for sin' figurally casts Christ in the role of the Levitical purification sacrifice that 'condemns sin in the flesh.'

echoes.text: Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.”
echoes.note: The flesh/Spirit antithesis (vv.5-9), where 'flesh' marks mortal humanity opposed to God's enduring Spirit, faintly recalls 'My Spirit will not abide in man forever, for he is flesh.'

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: 'The spirit is alive' / God giving 'life to your mortal bodies' (vv.10-11) faintly evokes the breath of life animating dust-formed Adam, now reapplied as resurrection-life by the Spirit.

echoes.text: For you are our Father, though Abraham doesn’t know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us: you, Yahweh, are our Father; our Redeemer from everlasting is your name.
echoes.note: 'You, O LORD, are our Father' — Israel's corporate address of God as Father — stands behind the Spirit-prompted filial cry 'Abba! Father!' (v.15).

echoes.text: “But I said, ‘How I would put you among the children, and give you a pleasant land, a goodly heritage of the armies of the nations!’ and I said, ‘You shall call me “My Father”, and shall not turn away from following me.’
echoes.note: 'I thought you would call me My Father and would not turn from following me' — God's hope that adopted Israel address him as Father — resonates with the adoptive cry of v.15.

echoes.text: I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.
echoes.note: The covenant formula 'I will... be your God, and you shall be my people,' realized through the indwelling Spirit (vv.9-16), faintly underlies the divine-belonging and sonship affirmed by the Spirit's testimony.

echoes.text: For as the rain comes down and the snow from the sky, and doesn’t return there, but waters the earth, and makes it grow and bud, and gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so shall my word be that goes out of my mouth: it shall not return to me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing I sent it to do.
echoes.note: The word/seed that goes out from God's mouth and does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, yielding seed and bread; the sower-and-word matrix governs the parable, made explicit in the later interpretation (v.19, 'the word of the Kingdom').

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem, “Break up your fallow ground, and don’t sow among thorns.
echoes.note: 'Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns' — the contrast of receptive ground vs. thorn-choked soil maps directly onto Jesus' soils; thorns that choke recur in v.7, 22.

echoes.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.
echoes.note: 'Sow righteousness... break up your fallow ground' — agricultural sowing-and-reaping imagery for response to God's word; thematic rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him.
echoes.note: Isaac sows and reaps a hundredfold (LXX 'hekatosteuousan') in the same year — the only clear OT 'hundredfold' agricultural blessing, possible backdrop for the good soil's hundredfold yield (v.8).

echoes.text: For as the husbandman sows much seed upon the ground, and plants many trees, and yet not all that is sown shall come up in due season, neither shall all that is planted take root: even so those who are sown in the world shall not all be saved.
echoes.note: Second Temple (4 Ezra): the farmer sows much seed but not all that is sown takes root or is saved — a near-contemporary Jewish sower parable of differential reception; cf. also 2 Esdras 9:31.

echoes.text: Let me sing for my well beloved a song of my beloved about his vineyard. My beloved had a vineyard on a very fruitful hill. He dug it up, gathered out its stones, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in its midst, and also cut out a wine press therein. He looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes. “Now, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, please judge between me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my […]
echoes.note: The Song of the Vineyard: God plants/sows expecting fruit and is disappointed by a barren yield; thematic kinship with fruit-bearing soils but no verbal overlap.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The sower went out to scatter the seed.
Some on the path, some on the rock, some in good soil.
Your word is a lamp to our feet.
A light to the road we walk.
Let the one with ears to hear, listen.
Open us, and let the seed take root.
Come, let us worship the God who plants.
We come; sow your word in us. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Picture the field at dawn, the sower's arm swinging wide, seed flying onto path and rock and rich dark ground.
Sow your word in us, and let it grow.
Some of us came hard-packed as a footpath, some shallow over stone, some choked by the week's thorns.
Sow your word in us, and let it grow.
But the sower is not stingy — he flings the seed everywhere, on every kind of ground, hoping.
Sow your word in us, and let it grow.
Your word is a lamp to our feet; let it fall on good soil today and bear thirty, sixty, a hundredfold.
Sow your word in us, and let it grow. Amen and amen!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The sower scatters seed on every kind of ground.
Sow your word in us, and let it grow.
Some of us are footpath, some stone, some thorns.
Sow your word in us, and let it grow.
Your word is a lamp to our feet on the road.
Sow your word in us, and let it grow.
Come, let us worship the God who plants in us.
Sow your word in us, and let it grow. Amen.

turn.gravity: Isaiah promises a word that goes out like rain and does not return empty; the Psalm soaks the furrows and crowns the year with bounty; and Jesus flings seed across every kind of ground. The nerve: the Word is already doing its work — the open question is the ground it lands on, and you are the ground.
turn.trap: It turns into a scolding to "be good soil" — as if dirt could improve itself — which is both impossible and tone-deaf to the wild generosity of the sowing. Or it becomes pure reassurance ("the Word never fails") that quietly ignores the three-quarters that bore nothing.
turn.hinge: The seed is flung with abandon on ground that cannot, by itself, change what it is — and still the call is to hear and bear fruit. The Sower's recklessness and the soil's responsibility both stand; drop either and the parable goes flat.

doors.claim: The four soils are a mirror held up to the hearer — the trodden path, the shallow rock, the choking thorns, the open field — and the sermon asks which you are today.

witnesses.author: Rabanus Maurus
witnesses.reading: The wayside is the mind trodden and hardened by the continual passage of evil thoughts, so that the seed cannot sink in.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: The deceitfulness of riches chokes the word, for riches are treacherous — promising one thing and doing another.

doors.say: The same seed fell on all four grounds; the difference was the soil — and the soil is you.
doors.do: Have each hearer name which ground their heart is this season, and the one thing trodding, drying, or choking the word in them.

doors.claim: No careful farmer sows on a footpath, on rock, in thorns — but this Sower scatters everywhere, and that abandon is the gospel: God writes off no ground.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: How is it reasonable to sow among thorns, on stony ground, by the wayside? In ordinary soil it would be folly — but the Sower casts the seed even there.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: By this Sower is meant the Son of God, who sows among the people the word of the Father.

doors.say: Look how prodigally God spends the seed — on the hardened, the shallow, the crowded — refusing to decide in advance which ground is hopeless.
doors.do: Turn them from writing off a hard "soil" in their life — a person, a place — to scattering the word there anyway.

doors.claim: Good soil is not just receptive but fruitful — it hears, understands, and yields; a faith that takes the word in and grows nothing is not yet the good ground.

witnesses.author: Remigius of Auxerre
witnesses.reading: These ears to hear are the ears of the mind — to understand, and to do the things that are commanded.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The good ground is the one who hears the word and considers it — in spite of Satan; it has deep root, and brings forth fruit in various proportions, some a hundredfold.

doors.say: The test of the word in you is not how warmly you received it but what it has grown.
doors.do: Send them to one concrete fruit the word is asking of them this month — and to tend it, not just admire the seed.

synthesis.convergence: Three of the readings sing of a Word and Spirit doing fertile, unstoppable work — rain that does not return empty (Isaiah 55), furrows soaked and the year crowned (Psalm 65), the Spirit giving life and freedom (Romans 8) — and the fourth asks only whether that seed finds root in us (the Sower).
synthesis.claim: God's word is already at work and will not come back empty; your part is not to manufacture the harvest but to be ground that lets it root.
synthesis.here: For anxious sowers — parents, teachers, pastors — who fear their labor falls on hard ground, the move is to trust the seed's own power and the Spirit's fertility: keep scattering, and tend the soil of your own attention rather than counting the yield.

turn.subtract: Three doors, three landings — self-examination (which ground), grace (the reckless Sower), fruitfulness (hearing that yields). Walk through one; the choosing is the focus.
turn.source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain) + Wesley's Explanatory Notes, retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
